# What It's Doing to You

> "Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint."
>
> — Proverbs 25:28

This is the chapter where the lies are thickest.

Most men, especially young and single ones, think they've already counted the cost of this habit and found it small. "It doesn't hurt anybody. The doctors say so." We settled the doctors back in the introduction. They're talking about your body, and on your body we take their word. **This book isn't about your body.**

A doctor can check your blood pressure. But who checks your drive, or your nerve? Who checks whether you can hold a woman's gaze, keep a promise to yourself, or pray without flinching? No clinic runs those tests. You're the only one who can read the results, and you've been reading them for years.

So almost nothing in this chapter is a medical finding, and at the one point where the doctors come into it I'll say so. The rest is conviction, and it is the testimony of men who lived it. Check every line against your own life. If one doesn't fit, drop it. I don't think you'll drop many.

Here's a thought experiment before we start. Suppose your phone lit up one night, just as you reached for it, with a message that said: "You've got away with it until now. Do it once more and the damage is permanent." Would you carry on?

You wouldn't. You'd put the phone in a drawer and go for a walk. Which shows that some part of you has been betting, every single night, that tonight's one doesn't count.

## A conversation {-}

I've had this conversation, in one form or another, with a lot of young men.

"Why do you want to stop?"

"I saw a video. Apparently a thirty-day streak makes you magnetic to women."

"Aren't you worried about what it's doing to you?"

"Not really. Anyway, I could be hit by a bus tomorrow."

"Would you walk out in front of one on purpose?"

"Obviously not."

"Do you look both ways before you cross the road?"

"Of course I do."

There you have it. He takes real care over a danger that will almost certainly never touch him, and he ignores the thing that touches him every night. He wouldn't board a plane if someone told him one bolt was loose. But a habit that is loosening his nerve, his attention and his self-respect a turn at a time doesn't worry him.

And what's he getting in exchange? NOTHING.

The young man doesn't notice, and there's a reason for it. At twenty he has energy to burn, nobody depending on him, and no wife lying beside him to notice that he's absent. He can fund the habit out of the surplus. The bill arrives later, when life starts asking for everything he has and he finds he's been spending a tenth of it in the dark for fifteen years.

## It isn't a landmine {-}

Men who do worry tend to picture the cost as a landmine. It's somewhere out in the field, and you might tread on it or you might not. So far, so good.

Get that picture out of your head. The cost isn't buried up ahead. **IT'S ALREADY BEING PAID.** It's taken out every time, in small coins, and that's why you never see the total.

I promised you no shock treatment, and I'll keep the promise. Nothing below will be news to you. It's a list of things you already know and have trained yourself not to look at.

**Your drive.** One coach did this daily for years, and he sums up what it does to men in three short sentences: "It kills their drive. It destroys their confidence and it numbs their hunger." Why would it do that? His answer is the one you met three chapters ago, and it's the best I've heard: it hands a man the reward without the effort. Think about what a man's hunger is for. It's meant to get him up, send him out and make him build something, win someone and become someone. Then every night he tells that hunger it has already been fed. After enough years it stops asking.

That is the flat feeling. It isn't sadness, exactly. It's being, in his words, "a zombie walking through life wondering where all your motivation went". You know the feeling. The morning after, you've got your coffee, your list and your good intentions, and there's nothing behind them. One man on the NoFap forum, ninety days out, remembered where he had been: "My drive for life was almost at zero."

It isn't only the gym coaches who say so. Listen to three men who have never met.

The first is a pastor, and married. God put the drive in a husband, he says, partly so that he would pursue his wife: date her, listen to her, win her again. Take that drive somewhere else, "even let's say mindlessly masturbating", and it's spent. "I don't have it anymore", he says, and the husband ends up with a book on one side of the room while his wife gets on with her evening on the other.

The second is a young Christian who fought this for nineteen years: "the purpose of lust is to make you comfortable". Comfortable, satisfied, content with where you are in your life. That is exactly what a man with something to build can't afford to be.

The third isn't religious at all. He was a broke actor whom the world ignored, by his own account, and he looked back and saw where the hunger had gone: "so many of us since we were like 12 years old had been killing that desire".

And a man on the NoFap forum, ninety days free, wrote the plainest version of the charge that I've found anywhere:

> "you fap your urges away, believing that you're fapping your stress away. Other than very temporarily, you're not. Guess what you are actually fapping away? Your manhood. Your desire to meet your obligations and carry out your responsibilities."
>
> — a man on the NoFap forum, ninety days free

He went on down the list: his self-esteem, his time, his relationships, his happiness.

**Your focus.** C.S. Lewis put it in three words: "indulgence brings fog". Ask the students. "I m not completely focused on my study", writes one. "I was kinda loosing my memory, I became very forgetful", writes another. Part of the fog is simple tiredness. A bigger part is that the habit takes up room in your head. A corner of your mind is always either planning the next time or regretting the last, and a man can't give his whole attention to anything while one corner of it is always busy somewhere else. Remember the man from the introduction who felt like he was "coming out from a fog"? He hadn't known he was in it until it lifted. Nobody does.

**Your confidence.** This is the one men find hardest to believe and easiest to recognise. Why would something done alone, behind a locked door, change how you stand in a room?

Because you bring it with you. You walk in knowing what you did at midnight, and you assume it shows. That first coach describes the morning after: you "can't even make eye contact with people cuz you're so disgusted with yourself". A married man told a sobriety forum what years of it had done:

> "I was becoming socially akward. Most times I didn't feel like talking to good old friends let alone strangers."
>
> — a man on a sobriety forum

It's worst around women. A man who spent last night using women in his head finds it hard to look the next real one in the eye this morning. He's either sizing her up or looking at his shoes. He's forgotten how to simply talk to her as a person, because he's had so much practice treating women as something else. The men who get out say that this changes too: "I feel like a better person and have a better appreciation for women".

**Your standing before God.** If you're a believer, you'll know this one best. If you're not, read it as "your conscience".

After Adam ate the fruit, the first thing he did was hide. God came walking in the garden, and Adam, who had walked with him every evening, was crouching in the bushes. Nobody had told him to hide. Shame did it without being asked.

That's the real cost of this habit to a Christian man, and it has nothing to do with lightning bolts. God doesn't leave. You do. You skip the prayer because of what you did an hour ago. You sit at the back and keep quiet in the small group. You feel like a fraud with a Bible in your hand. One young man said of those years:

> "During this time of my life I was not walking with God--I was crawling."
>
> — a 19-year-old, in a testimony on a Christian site

Another called it "the number one hindrance with my walk with God". A third found he couldn't even bear the music: "I was washing dishes listening to rock to avoid listening to worship music because the shame."

The pastor John Piper watched what this did to the young men around him. He saw them feel the pull to do something great with their lives, and he saw each one draw back because he felt unworthy and unable to obey the call of God. His conclusion was blunt: masturbation becomes the enemy of missions. You may never go abroad as a missionary. But you have a calling, whatever it is, and this habit has been telling you for years that you're not the sort of man who gets to answer it.

**Your marriage.** Or the marriage you hope to have.

Lewis saw this more clearly than anyone. Desire, he said, is meant to drive a man out of himself and towards a real woman, with all her otherness and her right to say no. The habit turns him round and sends him back, as you read in an earlier chapter, into the prison of himself with his harem of imaginary brides. The harem never has a headache, never needs listening to and never asks anything of him. And a man can come to prefer it that way, as a later chapter will show.

So the husband lies a foot from his wife and a hundred miles away. She can't name what's wrong, but she can feel that some part of him is being spent elsewhere. Sometimes his body tells on him. "I knew there was a serious problem", wrote the man from the sobriety forum, "when I was losing my erection sometimes when I was with my wife". Sometimes the guilt does the damage. One husband wrote of giving in and "then feeling like a great failure to God, her, and myself." And he can't tell her, so there's now a locked room in the marriage. Tim Challies described the whole sad exchange in a sentence: "It takes an act God intends to build relationship and makes it an act of selfish isolation."

A single man shouldn't imagine that a wedding ring will fix it. Ask any married man in the trap. He took the habit up the aisle with him.

**Your body, after all.** I said this book isn't about your body, and I said we take the doctors' word on it. Here is the one place where the doctors themselves have something to add.

Men have a slang name for it: death grip. Years of the same hard, hurried habit train a body to answer to one thing only, which is its owner's hand. Then a real woman arrives, and the body doesn't know her. Some men can't finish with her. Some can't stay ready. Sex therapists and urologists see these men regularly, and they have their own drier names for it.

A medical student told his story on the NoFap forum. With his first girlfriend, "even after months, still no orgasm for me. I couldn't even get close." Then comes the sentence every husband should read twice: "She started to think it was her fault, but deep inside, I knew what the problem was."

Another man on the same forum explained it better than a textbook: "The idea with MO is that it's a dress rehearsal for sex. When you train your body to respond to a stimulus sex can't replicate you will struggle to perform during sex." A urologist who has nothing against masturbation says of the effect on a couple: "it can be devastating".

Let's keep this honest. It isn't an official diagnosis, and nobody has proved the cause. One study of several hundred young men found that those with erection trouble were about twice as likely to masturbate in these rough ways, which shows a link and no more. Some doctors doubt it's common. And if this is your trouble, see a doctor, because medicines and other conditions can do the same thing.

But notice what the specialists prescribe, including the ones who say the habit is harmless. They tell these men to stop. And the medical student? A little over a month after he stopped: "I had an orgasm during sex, for the first time in my life." For other men it has taken many months. Nobody can promise you a date. What the men who stop do report is that the body, like the lawn, grows back.

## Both sides of the rope are fear {-}

We tend to picture a tug-of-war. One team is fear: "It's a sin, it's draining me, I hate the secrecy." The other team we think of as pleasure: "It's my comfort and my release, the one thing that's mine."

Look at that second team again, because it's fear as well. It isn't that you enjoy the habit so much. It's that you're uneasy without it. The man who never started isn't uneasy without it, any more than you're uneasy without a cigarette. The habit doesn't soothe that unease. It manufactures it.

This is also why a list of costs has never made you stop. A frightened man reaches for his comfort, and you know what you've trained yourself to reach for. So instead of stopping, men develop a set of dodges:

**"Every man slows down eventually. I'll be flat at fifty whatever I do."** Maybe so. Is that a reason to arrive early? And we're not talking about vigour here. We're talking about slavery.

**"It's my life. Better to enjoy it than to live like a monk."** Quite right, enjoy it. Now tell me honestly that the life you've read about over the last few pages is the enjoyable one. Tell me the man hiding in the bushes is having a better time than the man walking in the garden.

**"I'm single. Who exactly am I hurting?"** The man you're turning into. Your future wife will marry whatever comes out the other end of this. And apart from all that, there's you now. You're a person too.

## A city without walls {-}

Now read the proverb at the head of the chapter again.

In Solomon's day a city's wall was the city. Inside the wall were homes, markets, children playing and a temple. Take the wall away and you still have all those things, until the first raiding party arrives. A city without walls belongs to whoever turns up, however rich it is.

Solomon says a man without self-control is like that. He doesn't call him wicked or worthless. He calls him defenceless. Whatever turns up gets in: a mood, an image, a bad day, a pretty face on a screen. Such a man doesn't decide what happens in his own evening. You read the gym's version of the same thing in the introduction: "the more lust controls you the easier you are to control".

Here the thread that runs through this book comes out into the open. **A man who can't control his lust can't be trusted.**

That sounds harsh. It's only a description. His wife is trusting a man who keeps a locked room. His children are being raised by a man who's only half there. And the person who trusts him least is himself. Count the promises. "Never again." "This is the last time." "Starting Monday." You've made each of them in earnest, perhaps hundreds of times, and broken every one. The coach names the price: each time, "you break that promise you had with yourself."

A man can only break his word to himself so often before he stops believing it. After that, when he says "I'll start the business" or "I'll get fit" or "I'll be a better husband", something inside him quietly replies, "No, you won't. I know you." That is the deepest thing the habit does. It makes you a man whose word, in his own ears, is worth nothing.

Don't hear that as a verdict. Walls can be rebuilt, and Nehemiah put Jerusalem's back up in fifty-two days. Yours will go up faster, and you won't be straining at the stones, as you'll see. For now, just look at the gap in the wall and admit that it's there.

## So far, so good {-}

You've heard the one about the man who falls from the roof of a skyscraper. As he passes each floor, the people at the windows hear him say, "All right so far!"

That's how we reason. I've got away with it up to now, so one more can't matter. But the habit was never a string of separate nights. It's a chain, and each time makes the next more likely.

The first time you did it, you lit a fuse, and nobody told you how long it was. I can't tell you what's at the end of yours. For one man it's the evening his wife picks up his phone. For another it's the night his body won't answer when she reaches for him. For another it's the day the fantasy crosses a line he swore it never would, and he sits there afterwards not recognising himself. For many it's quieter than any of those: a fortieth birthday, and the cold realisation that the bold young man with all the plans never did any of them. A man of forty-three wrote that this habit had "destroyed four (4) marriages". He didn't see the end of the fuse coming, and he had four chances.

Every time is one more inch burned. **HOW DO YOU KNOW IT ISN'T THE NEXT ONE?**

## Sinister black shadows {-}

There's one more cost, and it's the one you'll be gladdest to lose.

Every man with this habit carries a shadow at the back of his mind. Most of the time he doesn't look at it. He jokes and works and sings on Sunday. But it's there, just under the surface, and it goes wherever he goes: the knowledge that he's doing something he despises and has arranged his life so as not to think about it. It's the small jolt when the sermon turns to purity, or the half-second of dread when someone borrows his phone. It's also that vague uneasiness late at night after a bad day, which he's always blamed on the day.

The day didn't cause it. Men without the habit don't carry that shadow. David knew it well: "When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long." (Psalm 32:3)

One commenter needed only nine words: "Masterbation turns a happy day into a sad day". The spelling is his. He is not wrong.

Some of the gains of stopping are ones you'll notice and enjoy on purpose: the time, the energy, the end of the whole silly business of making love to nobody. But the best of them is a thing you'll notice by its absence. One ordinary afternoon you'll realise that the shadow isn't there, and hasn't been for days. You'll have nothing to hide and nothing to dread.

Now, these last three chapters have been rather one-sided. They've gone on at length about what you gain by stopping and what the habit costs. A fair book should give both sides. So the next chapter sets out, in full, the advantages of jerking off.
